title: Registry locking and routing policy playbook
body:
Purpose
This is a practical playbook for platform engineers and on-call SREs describing how model registry locking (version pinning) should interact with runtime routing policies across regions and capacity tiers. It focuses on operational semantics, reconciliation order, and edge cases that caused incidents in the past (see PLAT-412).

Scope
- Model registry: artifacts, metadata (schema version, hardware compatibility tags, quantization fingerprint).
- Version pinning / locking: customer pin, route-level pin, rollout pins (canary, staged).
- Routing policies: latency-first, cost-first, geo-preferred, fallback tiers (hosted -> dedicated -> private).
- Multi-region: primary/secondary region routing and cross-region fallback.
- Control plane: decisions made by control plane on rollout, reconciliation and automatic fallbacks.

High-level rules (summary)
1) Single source of truth order: route config > customer pin > global default. Route config may include a 'pin_override' flag to permit temporary route-specific lock bypasses for emergency rollbacks.
2) Compatibility check first: before routing to an instance/version, runtime verifies registry compatibility matrix (schema, kv-cache layout, kv-version). If mismatched, runtime rejects and control plane records a 'compatibility-failure' event.
3) Reconciliation cadence: control plane computes desired assignments every 30s, but violations from runtime (e.g., incompatibility) trigger immediate re-evaluation with exponential backoff back into normal cadence.
4) Canary and staged rollouts must always include a compatibility assertion step and a pre-rollout dry-run policy to validate model artifact metadata across a representative set of hardware types.

Detailed behaviors and examples
A) Route-level pin vs Customer pin- If a route has an explicit pin to model v2.1 and the customer also has a broader account pin to v2.0, route-level pin wins for that route only. Documented exception: if control-plane detects v2.1 fails compatibility on critical region for the account, it will synthesize a temporary override and notify the route owner. (See decision flow below.)

B) Canary with cross-region fallback- Canary rollout to us-west only: 5% traffic to v3-canary in us-west, rest to v2-stable in all regions. If us-west reports high latency for v3-canary due to kernel-level quantization fallback, control plane will pause the canary and optionally route the 5% to v2-stable in us-west (no cross-region routing by default). If the primary region capacity is exhausted and a route allows cross-region fallback, control plane will consider routing to us-east but only if the registry indicates v2-stable has identical output-determinism metadata (checksum match) so we avoid quality regressions.

C) Emergency rollback pattern- When a pinned model causes an error spike:
- Step 1: Control plane evaluates if a higher-priority pin exists (route pin). If yes, it attempts to revert to that version.
- Step 2: If no higher-priority pin, evaluate last-known-good snapshot recorded in registry (timestamp + git-style commit id). If present, attempt immediate promotion.
- Step 3: If immediate promotion fails due to compatibility (rare), fall back to region-level serving policy (route->regional-compat-fallback: true/false). If false, escalate to on-call.

Compatibility matrix (operational view)
Columns: artifact_schema, kv_cache_layout, quant_fingerprint, supported_kernels, geo_affinity
Rows (examples):
- v2.0 | kv-v1 | q8_128 | cuda-11-x, cublasLt-2 | global
- v2.1 | kv-v2 | q8_128 | cuda-11-x, cublasLt-2 | global
- v3-canary | kv-v3 | q4_64  | cuda-12, lipsync-opt | us-west preferred
- v3-quantized | kv-v3 | q4_64  | cuda-12, quant-kernel-v1 | dedicated-gpu-pool

Notes on matrix usage:
- The runtime's compatibility check is a conservative match: exact kv_cache_layout match required; quant_fingerprint must be in allowed list for the selected kernel; supported_kernels is permissive (any overlap allowed) but a warning is emitted if only partial overlap.
- geo_affinity is advisory except when route policy declares 'hard_geo_pin'.

Decision flow (short)
1) Incoming request arrives.
2) Control plane resolves route -> candidate set (apply pin hierarchy).
3) Evaluate regional capacity & compatibility on candidate set.
4) If candidate passes compatibility and capacity, route immediately.
5) If candidate fails compatibility, mark event and attempt next candidate in priority. If none, follow fallback policy (fail, queue, or route to lower-quality model).

Edge cases and recommended mitigations
- Schema drift between minor versions: enforce a registry preflight CI that runs unit tests + a small inference sample against all runtime kernel types we support. Gate rollout if any kernel type fails.
- Mixed-precision mismatch: add explicit "safe-quantize" flag on registry entries; control plane rejects automatic fallbacks that would change quantization unless route allows it.
- Stale pins after model removal: periodically garbage-collect pins that reference deleted artifacts and notify route owners with a 30d grace window before auto-unpin.
- Orphaned per-route overrides after account-wide pin: track override metadata with TTL and require manual review if TTL expires.

Operational playbook snippets (runbook style)
- Alert: "compatibility-failure:high" in multiple regions -> run:
  1. Check latest control plane reconciliation logs for timestamp and failing regions.
  2. Identify whether the failing model is pinned (route or account).
  3. If pinned, follow emergency rollback pattern.
  4. If not pinned, consider traffic split rollback and open a PLAT incident.

Quick checklist for releasing a pinned model change
- Update registry metadata: include kv_cache_layout, quant_fingerprint, and list of supported_kernels.
- Run hardware matrix smoke tests (small-batch inference on each kernel/hardware).
- Create canary rollout with explicit compatibility gating.
- Monitor latency, error-rate, and output-diff metrics for 48h before broad promotion.

Open questions / follow-ups
- Do we want to allow an admin 'force-serve' that bypasses compatibility checks for debugging? (current leaning: yes, gated by audit + 2FA).
- How should we record deterministic output-diff tolerances in the registry (per-route vs global)?
- Tighten reconciliation documentation: should we expose reconciliation events to customer dashboards?

Appendix: example log snippet for a compatibility failure
2025-01-31T14:23:02Z control-plane reconcile route=chat-nlp-1 candidate=v3-canary region=us-west result=compatibility-failure reason=kv-mismatch expected=kv-v2 found=kv-v3
2025-01-31T14:23:03Z runtime us-west instance=gpu-23 reject model=v3-canary reason=kernel-missing kernel=lipsync-opt

Action items (owners)
- @Lars: add canary-preflight CI job to registry pipeline (PLAT-412) - due 2025-02-10.
- @Diego: implement compatibility-failure metrics and dashboard tiles - due 2025-02-17.
- @Priya: draft proposal for admin force-serve gating (doc + audit flow) - due 2025-02-07.

Notes to reviewer
This doc is intentionally pragmatic and includes several operational defaults we should validate with product and SRE. Looking for feedback on the conservative compatibility matching rules and whether geo-affinity should be promoted to a hard constraint in some enterprise tiers.
